Fair warning: this is mainly a rant

I made the decision to be healthier back in February. This included calorie counting, exercise, and eating healthier. When I started my family was supportive, but whenever I told them my goal weight (120-130 pounds) they thought it was "too thin". I told them about BMI and how a woman of my height has a healthy BMI in the range of 115-145 pounds, but they just get awkward and say "well.. ok", like they really don't believe me.

I can't gush to my grandma about what new size I fit into anymore, because she was all worried when I told her that I fit into a size 6. I don't know if it's because she thinks size 6 is the same size as it used to be when she was growing up, or if she just thinks its so small because she's so large.

Today I sent my husband a picture, and his first reply was "Sweetie, I can see your ribs are you still at a healthy weight?". I was clearly leaning back in the photo, and had to explain to him that yes I am still in the healthy BMI range (no where near the bottom in fact), and that when you lean back your ribs are going to be more prominent.

I started at 178 and am down to 140 now (woohoo!), and I feel like I can't gush to my family about my progress anymore. They think that I'll be "too thin" if I go lower, even though I'll still be a healthy weight. I plan on going lower anyway, but I just feel like they don't support me anymore.
My family is worried about me losing "too much" weight instead of being supportive, and it's frustrating.

Congrats!!! Family is weird... I told my mom that my goal weight is 145. (I'm 5'4", F, 195 and going down!) She freaked out, saying: " What??? 145 is so fat! How big are you???"

She is 110, btw... Yeah. Don't sweat it, just do what you know is best for your health and sanity. We will be cheering you on!!

Amythest Schaber is my favorite at the moment. They have a series called Ask an Autistic which is incredibly informative. It's was their videos that helped me recognize what as going on with me and seek out a professional diagnosis. I highly recommend them for anyone who is interested in hearing about autism from an autistic person's perspective.

I'm watching her now, but I don't know. Why does she keep saying "speaking with their mouth parts?" I also think this is the first time I've heard 'ableist' used outside of tumblrinaction. I'm 8 minutes into "What is Autism." Quite a few minutes were dedicated to "Autistic people are different. They learn differently. This makes them different. Society might do A, but autistic people are different, so they might do B or C or D."

Then again, I never knew someone could have autism and not show any visible signs (that I would catch, at least). She seems totally normal to me. Guess that shows how much I know about autism.

I think the "speaking with their mouthparts" thing is meant to distinguish that speech doesn't always have to be done verbally. Some people on the autism spectrum are non-verbal, so they cannot speak with their mouth, but many can speak using a computer (like Stephen Hawkings does, although he isn't autistic that I know of), or in writing. Many non-verbal people are treated as if they are mentally handicapped and that their voice doesn't matter, when in reality this is farthest from the truth. With autism, non-verbal does not necessarily mean mentally handicapped. Some of these people are trapped inside themselves, fully aware, and unable to communicate (ex. Carly Fleischmann). Truly a nightmare, if you ask me. So I guess, in a way, it's validating those who speak, but do so without their physical voice.

For me, her videos were incredibly helpful. I'm similar to her in that someone just looking at me walking down the street would have no idea I was different. I'm almost 30, and was just diagnosed within the last month or so, and that was after years upon years of seeking help from doctors and mental health professionals, because I just wasn't coping with life. But no one caught on to what was really happening until I was finally referred to an autism specialist. This unfortunately is extremely common in women on the autistic spectrum, because it can present differently in us, and research in higher functioning autism, such as Asperger syndrome, had been done mostly on men and boys up until recently.

Some of the ableist stuff isn't my style, but I can understand where they are coming from on that. When you're different, it can be hard to get along in society, but I think it goes both ways. Coexist! Either way, her videos helped me find myself and get the help I needed. For that, I am truly grateful.
